# The built environment and cancer survivorship: a scoping review

**Authors:** Naiyu Chen; Carol Mita; Ilkania M. Chowdhury-Paulino; Alaina H. Shreves; Cindy R. Hu; Li Yi; Peter James

**Affiliations:** 1.Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 2.Countway Library, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3.Nuffield Department of Population Health, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK | 4.Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics, National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA | 5.Department of Environmental Health, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 6.Department of Population Medicine, Harvard Medical School and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute

## Abstract

There are more than 32 million cancer survivors worldwide. The built environment is one of the contextual factors that may influence cancer survivorship. However, studies investigating the interdisciplinary field of the built environment and cancer survivorship are lacking.

To conduct a systematic review of the existing literature regarding the relationship between the built environment and cancer survivorship, identify any knowledge gaps, and recommend future research directions.

A systematic literature search was performed by searching OVID Medline, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science Core Collection.

Of 4,235 unique records identified, 26 studies met eligibility criteria. Neighborhood walkability and greenness were the most examined built environment characteristics among the included studies. Walkability was found to be associated with various cancer survivorship experience, including increased levels of physical activity, lowered body mass index, and improved quality of life. The association between greenness and cancer survivorship outcomes were inconsistent across the included studies. Additionally, studies have reported the relationship between light and noise pollution and sleep among cancer survivors. Regarding blue space, in one qualitative study, breast cancer survivors brought up the healing properties of water.

Our scoping review demonstrated a breadth of current cancer survivorship research in the field of neighborhood walkability and greenness, but fewer studies detailing other aspects of the built environment as defined by this review, such as light pollution, noise pollution, and blue space. We identified future research directions for those interested in this interdisciplinary field, which can provide insights for urban planners and policy makers on how to best leverage the built environment to promote the health and wellbeing of cancer survivors.

## Introduction

Cancer survivorship is defined as the health and well-being of a person starting at cancer diagnosis, continuing through treatment, and lasting until the end of life.1 Measures of survivorship outcomes include, but are not limited to, side effects of treatment, follow-up care, cancer recurrence, diagnosis of other cancers, pain and fatigue, and quality of life (QoL)1. Focus on survivorship within the cancer continuum started to gain traction in the 1960s, after cancer survival rates increased substantially as a result of advancements in cancer treatment and early detection cancer screenings.2,3 There are currently more than 18 million individuals who are living with cancer in the United States and more than 32 million worldwide.4 This number is projected to increase in the future, emphasizing the need for research that addresses the health and well-being of this vulnerable and less examined population within the cancer continuum.5

There has been an emerging body of research that links cancer risk and outcomes to the neighborhood built environment (referred to hereafter as “built environment”), which refers to the physical makeup of human dwelling and activity, where we live, learn, work, and play.6,7 The built environment includes various features and characteristics such as neighborhood walkability, proximity to green space and blue space, transportation options, and exposure to noise and light pollution.6–9 Compared to individual- and interpersonal-level factors associated with cancer survivorship, the built environment presents itself as a unique opportunity for modifiable change that could be implemented on a contextual and more impactful scale. Prior interventions related to the built environment have been implemented for other public health issues, such as injury prevention and other chronic health outcomes.10,11 Given its modifiability combined with its ubiquity and almost inseparable connection to various aspects of people’s lives, the built environment could also serve as a point of intervention on a large scale that may positively impact the wellbeing of cancer survivors. However, the focus in the intersection of the built environment and cancer research currently revolves around cancer incidence and mortality, with a notable underrepresentation in aspects of cancer survivorship.6,12–14

This scoping review addressed the need to summarize the current findings on the built environment’s role in the survivorship experience of individuals with cancer. The primary objective was to systematically search and summarize the existing literature concerning the relationship between the built environment and cancer survivorship. In doing so, we aimed to identify knowledge gaps for researchers in this interdisciplinary field and provide recommendations for future research directions in this area.

## Methods

### Eligibility Criteria

To be included in the review, the study needed to be an experimental or observational study, be written in English, and conducted within human subjects only. To maintain robustness in the studies that we reviewed, we included peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, and conference/meeting abstracts, while excluding reviews, editorials, or opinion pieces. Both quantitative and qualitative studies were considered to capture the full breadth of literature focused on this topic. In terms of built environment factors, studies needed to focus on at least one of the following: (1) neighborhood greenness, (2) blue space, (3) neighborhood walkability, (4) light pollution, or (5) noise pollution. This pre-defined list was chosen based on their hypothesized mechanisms that link these factors with health promotion.6,15,16 To specifically focus our scope within the built environment, we did not include additional factors that may also overlay with an individual’s social environment, such as neighborhood quality, access, and neighborhood socioeconomic status. We excluded studies that focused on short-term (e.g., hours, days) interventions in an institutionalized setting (e.g., hospital based, nursing facility based) related to the built environment, because those were fundamentally different from the larger scale, contextual level built environment alterations that could be implemented on the policy level. In terms of cancer survivorship, studies needed to focus on survivorship experiences in any cancer types, excluding non-melanoma skin cancer. We excluded studies that only focused on cancer survival or mortality without mentioning any other outcome measures related to cancer survivorship experience. This is to treat cancer survivorship as an independent attribute focusing on the quality of their lived experience as cancer survivors, differentiating it from a mere focus of cancer mortality as the endpoint.

### Search Strategy

Studies discussing survivorship of individuals with cancer being exposed to selected aspects of the built environment were identified by searching MEDLINE (National Library of Medicine, Ovid), Embase (Elsevier, embase.com), Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL Complete, EBSCOhost), and Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate) on November 10, 2022. Controlled subject vocabulary terms (i.e. MeSH, Emtree, CINAHL thesaurus subject headings) were included when available and appropriate. The search strategies were designed and carried out by a research librarian (CM). A language limit was applied to include studies published in English. No publication date restrictions were applied. The exact search terms used for each of the databases are provided in Appendix 1.

### Selection Process

Screening was performed using the Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation Ltd., Melbourne, Australia). All reviewers (NC, IC, AS) worked in pairs to independently screen the titles, abstracts, and full text of all retrieved studies. Specifically, one reviewer (NC) screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved studies, while another independent reviewer (studies divided among IC and AS) screened for consensus. The same process was applied to screening the full text of all potentially eligible studies based on the initial title and abstract screening. After each stage of the screening, all reviewers met to discuss the screening results and, in the case of disagreements, a third reviewer served as the tiebreaker.

### Data Extraction

Data extraction was completed using a self-designed form housed in Covidence. All reviewers (NC, IC, AS) and the data extraction team (NC, IC, AS, CH, LY) contributed to developing the data extraction template. The data extracted included study characteristics (e.g., publication type, publication year, population), built environment measures (e.g., exposure/intervention, measurement, and categorization), cancer survivorship outcomes (e.g., cancer type, survivorship outcome measure definition), analysis methods, and main results. The data extract template is provided in Appendix 2. Members from the data extraction team worked in pairs to complete data extraction. In the case of disagreement, reviewers discussed with a third reviewer to reach agreement.

## Results

6,973 records were retrieved by the literature searches on November 10, 2022. Duplicates were removed using EndNote software (Clarivate, Philadelphia, PA), resulting in 4,346 references to import into Covidence. 78 additional duplicates were identified by Covidence and 33 duplicates were identified manually, resulting in 4,235 unique references for screening (Figure 1). 4,187 studies were excluded for not meeting eligibility criteria based on title and abstract screening. During the full text screening, 22 studies were excluded. Reasons for exclusion included wrong setting (i.e., in institutionalized settings), wrong outcomes (i.e., outcomes not pertinent to cancer survivorship), wrong comparator (i.e., compared cancer patients with the general public rather than with cancer patients in different levels of built environment factors), wrong intervention (i.e., interventions or exposures not considered as one of the five built environment factors of interest), and wrong study design (i.e., an experimental or observational study not conducted within human subjects). As a result, 26 studies were included in the review (Table 1).

Descriptive characteristics of the included studies are presented in Table 2. Out of the 26 studies, 23 were published in academic journals and 3 were meeting abstracts. Most were quantitative studies (N = 23), while the rest were qualitative studies (N = 3). The year of publication for the included studies ranged from 2003 to 2022, with 2 published before 2010, 4 published between 2010 and 2014, 8 published between 2015 and 2019, and 12 published in 2020 and onwards. Most studies were cross-sectional studies (N = 19), while the longitudinal studies were either cohort studies (N = 5) or randomized controlled trials (N = 2). Except for 1 study that did not specify, the included studies encompassed various geographic regions, including North America (N = 21), Europe (N = 2), and Asia (N = 2). Sample size for the included studies varied: less than 50 for 5 studies, between 50 and 1000 for 9 studies, between 1000 and 5000 for 8 studies, and larger than 5000 for 1 study.

Each of the 5 built environment measures considered by this review were examined by at least 1 included study. Most studies examined neighborhood walkability (N = 16) and greenness (N = 13) either individually or together. There were 2 studies that examined light pollution, and 1 study each examining noise pollution or blue space. Most studies examined multiple cancer sites (N = 14), while some studies were conducted among individuals with breast (N = 5), prostate (N = 2), kidney (N = 1), or skin cancer (N = 1) only. The most examined cancer survivorship experience measure was physical activity (PA) (N = 10), followed by QoL (N = 6), body mass index (BMI) (N = 3), sleep (N = 2), fatigue (N = 2), and others, including frailty, tumor free years, healing, mental health, and COVID-19 infection (N = 5).

### Neighborhood Walkability

Neighborhood walkability (referred to hereafter as “walkability”) is usually defined as an objective summary measure comprising some or all of the following built environment measures: population density, street connectivity, traffic density, residential density, land-use mix, sidewalk coverage, and business density17,18. These measures of walkability describe how easy it is to walk in a given neighborhood to accomplish everyday tasks. Some proposed mechanisms that link neighborhood walkability and wellbeing include increasing PA, improving physical health outcomes, and promoting social interactions and sense of community.17,19–21 For this review, as long as the study examined some component of walkability, it was included in the review. Most studies assessed walkability objectively, using Census data with geographic information system, Google Street View data, or other publicly available data sources (N = 10; Study Number: 3, 6, 8, 9, 14, 17, 20, 21, 22, 23). Some assessed walkability subjectively through conducting qualitative interviews or administering self-reported validated surveys, such as the Neighborhood Environment Walkability Scale (N = 4; Study Number: 5, 16, 19, 25). Two studies assessed walkability both objectively and subjectively (Study Number: 24, 26). For survivorship outcomes, most studies examined PA (N = 8; Study Number: 5, 14, 16, 17, 19, 24, 25, 26), followed by QoL (N = 3; Study Number: 3, 8, 21), other factors (N = 3; Study Number: 6, 9, 22), and BMI (N = 2; Study Number: 20, 23).

For studies examining PA outcomes, a majority found that higher walkability was associated with higher levels of PA. A study conducted among adult survivors of childhood cancers found that those who lived in a more walkable neighborhood, measured both objectively and subjectively, were more likely to have higher activity levels.22 Similarly, lower traffic density and larger perceived land use mix-diversity (i.e., greater number of shops within walking distance from home) were associated with meeting recreational PA recommendations.18,23,24 In two qualitative studies, participants mentioned their preferred quality and safety levels of the sidewalks when walking.25,26 Older participants preferred higher-quality, safer sidewalks to reduce the risk of falling. However, a study conducted among prostate cancer survivors found no associations between walkability and PA and another study conducted among rural cancer patients found that lower street connectivity was associated with meeting PA recommendations.27,28

Two studies examined BMI and found consistent results. One found that higher traffic density was associated with being overweight, while lower population density was associated with being obese.29 Similarly, the other study showed that, after adjusting for individual and neighborhood-level characteristics, the BMI of survivors residing in neighborhoods with the highest Neighborhood Walkability Index score quartile was 1.70 kilogram per meter squared lower than the BMI of survivors in neighborhoods in the lowest quartile.30

Among studies that examined QoL, both physical and mental QoL outcomes were examined. In a registry-based study conducted in California, participants living in the highest population density (vs. lowest population density) had lower physical and mental QoL.31 A separate study conducted among non-metastatic breast cancer patients found that living on streets with high-quality (vs. poor-quality) sidewalks was associated with better emotional QoL.32 This study also reported proximity to hospitals and perceived accessibility to business locations were found to be predictors of cancer patients’ QoL, while population density and intersection density showed weak associations in terms of statistical significance level and effect size.33

There were also studies that examined walkability with other survivorship outcomes, including COVID-19 infection rate, tumor free years, and frailty. In a study conducted among individuals receiving cancer treatment in New York City, the odds of SARS-CoV-2 infection were higher in neighborhoods with higher population density compared to neighborhoods with lower population density.34 Among patients seeking radiotherapy and chemotherapy, both higher population density and intersection density were associated with reduced tumor-free years, but the results were not statistically significant.35 Lastly, among cancer survivors, reduced access to exercise opportunities was associated with higher prevalence of being pre-frail and frail compared to being non-frail.36

### Neighborhood Greenness

The proposed mechanisms for neighborhood greenness (referred to hereafter as “greenness”) include increased PA, improved social engagement, reduced stress, and decreased exposure to air pollution and extreme temperatures.15,17,37 There were 6 included studies that measured greenness, or neighborhood vegetation, objectively or subjectively. Objective measures of greenness included using geocoded satellite data (NavTEQ, Landsat) to identify natural environments and pre-specified forest therapy interventions (N = 6; Study Number: 3, 10, 11, 12, 14, 18). Measurements of perceived greenness included using qualitative interviews or self-reported perceived greenness or other surveys, including the Nature Relatedness Scale (N = 6; Study Number: 1, 4, 5, 7, 15, 25). One study examined greenness both objectively and subjectively (Study Number 26). Among these studies with neighborhood greenness as the exposure, most studies examined PA as the cancer survivorship outcome (N = 6; Study Number: 5, 11, 14, 15, 25, 26), followed by QoL (N = 4; Study Number: 1, 3, 10, 18), fatigue (Study Number: 4), BMI (Study Number: 12), and healing (Study Number: 7).

For studies that examined PA, many studies found that greenness exposure was not associated with meeting PA guidelines for cancer survivors and also not associated with either total PA levels or sports/leisure PA levels.18,23,38 A study that used nature relatedness, an individual’s affective cognitive and physical relationship with the natural world, as a proxy of greenness exposure found that those who were physically active had a higher score for nature relatedness compared to those who were inactive.39 In two qualitative studies, survivors mentioned that greenness during walks provided a sense of motivation and also shade was considered desirable while walking.25,26

The results related to QoL were inconsistent across the included studies. One randomized controlled trial found significant improvements in both physical and emotional well-being among breast or lung cancer patients who had undergone a three-week forest therapy intervention.40 In a qualitative study conducted in Sweden, participants mentioned that nature had been an important resource for coping and feeling better during their cancer survivorship.41 Individuals mentioned that walking outdoors and listening to “natural music” (i.e., birdsongs and the wind) were beneficial coping factors. However, results from quantitative studies were inconsistent. In a study by Chu et al., participants living near parks had lower mental composite scores. Conversely, Gorin et al. found that individuals living near green space and farmlands were positively associated with mental composite score and negatively associated with physical composite scores.31,42

There were also studies that examined greenness with other survivorship outcome measures, including BMI, fatigue, and healing. Compared to those not living in rural areas, survivors living in a rural area were at an increased risk of having higher BMI.43 However, a study found that a natural restorative environmental intervention, which includes activities involving nature in some way that may help to rest and restore concentration and mental energy, resulted in reduced fatigue. Another study found that the presence of nature inspired feelings of calmness among a group of breast cancer survivors.44,45

### Light Pollution

Light pollution is thought to impact wellbeing via circadian rhythm disruption and hormone disregulation.46,47 The two included studies that examined light pollution both focused on sleep quality and one of the studies also examined fatigue and depression as survivorship outcome measures.48,49 Both studies used Actilight, which is a device that objectively measures light intensity in lux, to assess light exposure.48,49 Bernatchez et al measured minutes of light exposure larger than 1000 lux averaged across 7 consecutive days among advanced cancer patients, while Sun et al. measured both minutes of light exposure larger than 1000 lux over a 3-day period and intensity of light exposure among cancer outpatients. However, both studies only broadly measured out-of-bed light exposure and did not differentiate between light exposure during the day and light exposure at night.

Bernatchez et al. found that higher 24-hour light exposure was associated with lower subjectively measured wake after sleep onset and greater subjectively measured sleep efficiency. This is consistent with the results in Sun et al., where both greater minutes of light exposure and intensity of light exposure were associated with better sleep quality. Additionally, Sun et al. found that greater minutes of light exposure were associated with lower fatigue symptoms, assessed using the Brief Fatigue Inventory-Taiwan that was developed specifically for cancer patients, and greater intensity of light exposure is associated with lower fatigue symptoms and depression severity.

### Noise Pollution

Noise pollution is proposed to act through the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and sympathetic nervous system, which then may result in increased stress hormone levels and disturbance of sleep.50–52 One study examined the association of noise exposure and sleep quality among patients with advanced cancer receiving palliative care.49 In this study, bedroom nocturnal noise exposure was objectively measured using a sound level meter, which recorded data every minute for seven days. Using the World Health Organization’s recommendations, the study defined sound greater than 45 decibels during the night as noise pollution. The outcomes of interest were sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, early morning awakening, total time in bed, sleep efficiency, and number and duration of naps. These sleep measures were measured subjectively using the Sleep and Pain Diary and Insomnia Severity Index and objectively using Actigraphy. Nocturnal noise in the bedroom was significantly associated with a lower subjective and objective time in bed, which showed that reduced noise pollution within the bedroom was correlated with better sleep among cancer survivors.

### Blue Space

Blue space refers to man-made or planned exposure to bodies of water, including ponds, rivers, lakes, and the ocean.53,54 Some hypothesized pathways that link blue space and health include increased levels of PA and improved restoration of psychological wellbeing.16 One qualitative study explored the relationship between blue space and its role in cancer survivorship among breast cancer survivors.45 In the interviews, a recurring theme was the healing properties of water. Three out of the 14 women included in the study had mentioned that being located near a body of water was therapeutic in their healing. Specific qualities of water that were found to contribute to psychological well-being included the smell of sea air and the feeling of physically being in water.

## Discussion

In this scoping review, we identified 26 studies that examined the role of the built environment and cancer survivorship. Our search demonstrated a breadth of current cancer survivorship research in the field of neighborhood walkability and greenness, but also literature gaps in other aspects of the built environment as defined by this review, such as light pollution, noise pollution, and blue space. Inconsistencies in current findings also presented opportunities for future directions within this area of research.

For neighborhood walkability, most studies consistently found that higher walkability was associated with higher levels of PA and lower BMI in cancer survivors. However, findings were inconsistent regarding walkability and the QoL among cancer survivors, where one study found null associations, and another found greater improvements in well-being among women with breast cancer who lived in neighborhoods with low-quality (vs. high-quality) sidewalks. One explanation could be that the inconsistent studies were examining different components within walkability, including population density, street connectivity, and business density.31,32 While increasing the level of walkability, higher population density might negatively impact QoL if it is related to crowding within living spaces, but higher street and business density might positively impact QoL through promoting walking and PA. Future studies are suggested to investigate both the composite and individual components of walkability and its impact on cancer survivorship, particularly on QoL.

For neighborhood greenness, the results across studies were generally inconsistent for different cancer survivorship outcome measures. This could be due to the diverse but inconsistent measures of greenness across the studies. Among objective measures, proxies of greenness ranged from crude definitions, such as rurality, to more specific ones, such as percent greenness captured by geocoded satellite data. Among the subjective measures, definitions of greenness also varied greatly. In some cases, nature was used to broadly describe greenness, which could include a mix of greenness and natural environments not necessarily built by humans.41 Reliance on crude proxies of greenness could be partly attributed to the low utilization of objective satellite measures of greenness and limited computational power to conduct geographic information systems analyses in older studies. Future studies should utilize more consistent measures for greenness to allow for better comparability across studies.

Studies looking at exposures to light, noise, and blue space are still limited. Based on the few studies that were identified by our search, there was preliminary evidence showing their potential roles in the survivorship experience among cancer patients. Also, the two studies examining light pollution did not distinguish between light at night and general daytime light, or sun, exposure. It might be worth differentiating the two in future studies as light at night, specifically, was found to be associated with increased cancer risks, so it might independently play a harmful role in cancer survivorship as well.13,55 In addition, based on the current findings regarding blue space and wellbeing within the general population, future studies could examine its role quantitatively and look into specific aspects of blue space that particularly impact cancer survivors.16

### Strength and Limitations

The included studies had some shared strength. While there were 2 studies conducted before 2010, most of the studies were conducted more recently, with the majority published in the last 5 years. The included studies also had some common limitations. The majority of the studies were cross-sectional studies, so temporality between the built environment factors and cancer survivorship measures cannot be determined. Even among studies that were longitudinal, the duration of the study period was short, ranging from weeks to less than 3 months. This demonstrated a need for longitudinal studies that span across a longer study period to examine the long-term impact or proper windows of susceptibility of the built environment on cancer survivorship. Lastly, many studies conducted unadjusted analysis and reported associations or unadjusted means as their outcome measures.

One limitation of this scoping review was that we specifically examined a pre-defined list of five built environment factors. Other built environment factors, such as neighborhood quality or neighborhood socioeconomic status, were not included in this review given our choice to exclude factors that may overlap with the social environment. As described in the Methods section and Appendix 1, we chose to focus on these five built environment factors as a starting point and not expand our search to other factors that may also incorporate interpersonal-level factors that are not relevant to the objective of this review. Though beyond the defined scope of this review, we recognize that these additional built environment factors could also play a role in cancer survivorship.56,57 Additionally, we did not include non-English literature.

Our scoping review also had some notable strengths. First, this was one of the first reviews to specifically examine the built environment and cancer survivorship outcomes. Both fields are fairly novel areas of research on their own and the intersection of the two is even more innovative. Second, this review included all studies that were conducted on this topic in the peer-reviewed literature prior to November 10, 2022. Not imposing a publication date restriction allowed us to classify the trajectory of growth in research on this topic. Third, this review encompassed a wide array of study types, including randomized controlled trial, cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and qualitative studies. The inclusion of diverse study types facilitated a more holistic understanding around this topic. Lastly, we focused on a diverse range of cancer survivorship outcome measures, including physical and mental quality of life, sleep, and more, providing more informative and nuanced findings on the quality of cancer survivors’ lived experience that is not captured by cancer mortality.

### Conclusion

The significance of the role of built environment in the cancer continuum is being increasingly recognized, as evidenced by the emerging body of research that investigates this interdisciplinary junction.6 Literature specific to the built environment and cancer survivorship is underrepresented but gaining traction, with a growing number of studies published in recent years. Our scoping review summarized findings from existing literature and identified future research directions for those interested in this interdisciplinary field. This scoping review motivated the need for future work in identifying subgroups defined by built environment factors that may be vulnerable to unfavorable cancer survivorship outcomes and in generating hypotheses for interventions related to the built environment that could bring large scale changes to this vulnerable population. Urban planners and policy makers can then utilize findings from these studies to best leverage the built environment to promote the health and wellbeing of cancer survivors.

## Abstract

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is a major source of mortality and is the first manifestation of heart disease for most cases. Thus, there is a definite need to identify risk factors for SCD that can be modified on the population level. Short-term exposures to temperature have been implicated as a potential risk factor. Our objective was to determine if short-term temperature exposures were associated with increased risk of SCD in a US-based time-stratified case-crossover study.

A total of 465 cases of SCD were identified among participants of the prospective Nurses’ Health Study (NHS). Control days were selected from all other matching days of the week within the same month as the case day. Average ambient temperature on the current day (Lag0) and preceding 27 days (Lags1–27) was determined at the residence level using 800-m resolution estimates. Conditional logistic distributed lag nonlinear models (DLNMs) were used to assess the relative risk (RR) of the full range of temperature exposures over the lag period.

Warmer exposures in the days before event and colder temperatures 21–28 days prior were associated with increased risks of SCD. These results were driven by associations in regions other than the Northeast and among married women.

Both warm and cold ambient temperatures are suggestively associated with risks of SCD among middle-aged and older women living across the United States.

Keywords: Sudden cardiac death, Mortality, Heart disease, Risk factors

## What this study adds

This study adds to a growing body of literature that short-term temperatures are a population-level risk factor for sudden cardiac death (SCD). It adds to the limited body of evidence on the impacts of nonextreme temperatures on SCD and suggests that both warm and cold temperatures are associated with an increasing risk of SCD.

## Introduction

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) accounts for approximately 180,000–400,000 deaths in the United States each year.1–3 The lifetime risk of SCD has been estimated to be 10.9% among men and 2.8% among women, although lifestyle factors (e.g., blood pressure) only explain some of this risk.4 Therefore, there is a need to identify risk factors that can be modified on a population level to broadly impact SCD risk.

Seasonal patterns in cardiovascular incidence and mortality have been observed in countries around the world,5,6 with consistently higher disease incidence in winter months.7,8 Although many studies have observed this pattern for SCD as well,7–10 some studies have observed higher incidence of SCD in the summer.9,11–16 Exposures to extreme temperatures have also been associated with increased odds of SCD or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in multiple study settings.7,8,16–44 Less is known, however, on the impact of more moderate temperatures on SCD or on associations in United States populations.13,45 Our objective was to examine the association between short-term temperature and changes in temperature with risks of SCD in women living throughout the United States. We also wanted to examine these associations among subpopulations (defined by region, season, and marital status [as a measure of socioeconomic status]).

## Methods

### Study population

The Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) is a prospective cohort study that began in 1976 with 121,701 married female registered nurses, 30–55 years of age, who each completed a mailed questionnaire. At the study inception, the nurses resided in 11 states (CA, CT, FL, MA, MD, MI, NJ, NY, OH, PA, and TX); however, due to residential mobility, there are now at least 10 cohort members in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Follow-up questionnaires, with response rates above 90%, are mailed every 2 years to update information on risk factors and the occurrence of major illnesses.46,47 Information on residential address is updated for each questionnaire, enabling residential mobility over follow-up to be accounted for. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and implied consent was inferred from the return of questionnaires.

### Sudden cardiac death case ascertainment

Deaths in the cohort are identified by reports from next of kin, postal authorities, or by searching the National Death Index (NDI). Details on the method of classifying SCD in this cohort have been published previously.3 Briefly, SCDs were confirmed by physician review of medical records and next-of-kin reports regarding the circumstances surrounding the death if not adequately documented in the medical record. Cardiac deaths were considered sudden if the death or cardiac arrest occurred within 1 hour of the onset of symptoms. To increase specificity for arrhythmic death, we also required there be no evidence of circulatory collapse or a neurologic event before the disappearance of the pulse.48 Unwitnessed deaths or deaths that occurred during sleep where the participant was documented to be symptom free within the preceding 24 hours were considered probable SCDs if an autopsy or circumstances suggested that the death could have been arrhythmic.49 SCD follow-up included all cases from the start of the cohort through the end of 2012. We excluded cases without complete information on date of death (n = 6) and those (n = 27) that occurred before temperature data were available.

### Short-term exposures to temperature

Gridded (800-m resolution) daily ambient temperature data from 1981 to 2012 were obtained from the Parameter-Elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group time series datasets50 from the Northwest Alliance for Computational Science & Engineering (NASCE).51 The predictions were produced from climatologically aided interpolation, have been shown to predict accurately (r2 = 0.99 and mean absolute error = 1.49 °F) when compared with weather station values, and have determined to be highly useful for environmental epidemiology studies.52 Briefly, temperature data from all weather stations across the conterminous United States from 1981 onward were compiled into a weighted regression model, accounting for elevation and other climatological factors, to produce grid-level daily average surface air temperature. Ambient average daily temperature data were assigned to each participants’ residential addresses for the 27 days before each case and control day.

### Statistical methods

We used a nested time-stratified case-crossover design to assess the associations of temperature on the current day (Lag0), the preceding 27 days (Lags1–27), the preceding week (average of Lags0–6), and previous weeks (average of Lags7–13, average of Lags14–20, and average of Lags21–27) with risk of SCD.53,54 Control days were selected to include all other matching days of the week within the same calendar month. The case-crossover design has been shown to effectively control for interindividual personal characteristics (e.g., age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and confounders; the time-stratified approach additionally controls for other potential confounders that vary with time, including lifestyle factors, seasonality, and long-term secular trends. Therefore, our models do not adjust for personal characteristics.

We performed conditional logistic regression stratifying on the matched set to obtain relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each of the week averages. For comparability across measures, we present RRs for an interquartile range (IQR) increase in temperature. Deviations from linearity in the dose-response were assessed through the use of cubic regression splines.55 Likelihood ratio tests comparing the model with the spline to a linear model were used to determine statistically significant deviations from linearity. To assess the overall impact of exposures from the current day to 27 days prior, we used distributed lag nonlinear models (DLNMs).56 The models included natural splines with 3 degrees of freedom each for temperature and the lag periods.

To assess potential effect modification by season (spring, summer, fall, and winter), region (Northeast: yes/no), and marital status (married: yes/no, as a proxy for socioeconomic status), we calculated the DLNM within strata. A two-sided P value of 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed in SAS, version 9.4, or R, version 4.3.1.

The average age at the time of SCD was 73.4 (SD = 6.5) years, and events were least likely to happen in the fall and on Wednesdays.

## Discussion

In this study of women from the US general population, increasing temperatures on the days before an event and decreasing temperatures almost a month prior were suggestively associated with increased risk of sudden cardiac death. These associations were driven by participants living outside the Northeast and by those who were married.

Our findings of an impact of temperature on SCD are consistent with the international literature on this topic,8,13,16,19,20,22,37,38,44,45,57 although many studies have focused specifically on temperature extremes.7,19,37,38,45,57 An early study in Canada found that among men under 65 years of age, cold snaps (defined as days on which the mean temperature was at least 4.4 °C lower than the day before) were associated with 16% increase in the number of SCDs.7 Similar findings were shown in a Tunisian study, where there was an increase in SCD when temperatures dropped below 15 °C.8 In a series of Finnish case-crossover studies conducted within The Finnish Study of Genotype and Phenotype Characteristics of Sudden Cardiac Death (FinGesture), exposures to cold spells (defined as 3 or more consecutive days with a daily minimum temperature below the fifth percentile for that address 1961–2011) in the 7 days preceding the death were consistently associated with an increased odds of SCD (odds ratio [OR] = 1.33 [95% CI = 1.00, 1.78]). These associations were strongest for longer cold spells, in autumn and winter, and in those with prior ischemic heart disease and not taking cardioprotective medications, and in those with higher levels of coronary stenosis.37,38,57 In a study of 243 sudden cardiac deaths in Israel, a ratio of observed to expected deaths of 1.20 (listed as not statistically significant) was observed for temperatures <15 °C on the day of event, compared with 1.00 for temperatures of 15–30 and 0.75 for temperatures >30. Associations were stronger among those with known heart disease.9 The findings of these studies are in alignment with our findings at both ends of the temperature range. In a Taiwanese study among patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia/cardiomyopathy, a total of 68 SCDs were confirmed by autopsy. SCDs peaked in summer months, increasing temperature on the day of the event (OR = 1.23 [95% CI = 1.16, 1.31], per SD increase) was associated with odds of SCD, after adjustment for other meteorological factors (e.g., sunshine duration, humidity).20 Among SCDs identified from autopsies in Budapest, Hungary (1995–2002), there was a negative correlation between daily mean temperature and number of SCDs.14 A negative correlation between minimum daily temperature sudden cardiac deaths was observed in Tokyo between 2012 and 2013.58 There have also been numerous studies that have observed increases in SCD with both hot and cold temperatures,19,22 indicating that there are complex patterns between SCD and temperature that vary around the world. In one of only a few studies on this topic in the United States, the relative risk of SCDs occurring in Olmstead County, MN was elevated in all seasons relative to the summer and in colder (below 17 °C) temperatures.13 In a study using daily mortality data from 50 US cities, exposures to both cold (daily maximum temperature less than or equal to the first percentile) and hot (daily minimum temperature ≥99th percentile) days were associated with increases in cardiac arrest deaths, and there was evidence that these associations were modified by average temperatures and temperature variability, availability of heating and cooling.45

An association between short-term exposures to temperature and SCD is biologically plausible through multiple mechanisms. These have previously been summarized by Ryti et al. and include changes in blood composition factors, changes in blood pressure, changes in autonomic function, changes in cardiac oxygen demand, and changes in endothelial function.57 For example, in studies where individuals were exposed to a few hours of moving air to induce cooling, increases in platelets, red blood cells, fibrinogen, cholesterol, and blood viscosity were observed, with larger increases in elderly participants compared with young adults.59,60 Similar effects have also been observed in studies of individuals subjected to high temperatures.61 Blood pressure has also been shown to vary with ambient temperature, with evidence of higher blood pressure in colder, as opposed to warmer, temperatures.60,62–64 Exposures to extreme temperatures have also been shown to alter autonomic function and that this dysregulation increases with age.65,66 Lastly, emerging evidence suggests that extremes in short-term temperature exposures are associated with ventricular arrhythmias, which may underlie the findings observed with SCD.67–69

Our study has several limitations. We do not have information on time-activity patterns for participants, and we do not know how well ambient temperature predictions predicted personal temperature exposures in this cohort. This would likely lead to nondifferential exposure misclassification, which would limit our power to detect statistically significant effects. The cohort is comprised of females who at enrollment were married and had a nursing degree. This potentially limits generalizability, especially if there are biological mechanisms that are not as relevant for men or for populations with different distributions of ambient temperature exposures. Lastly, although our study is comprised of one of the largest prospective collections of SCDs among women, due to the rarity of the event in an all female general population sample, power was limited to detect effects.

The study also has numerous strengths. This is one of only a small number of studies to examine the associations between short-term temperature exposures across a wide range of temperatures and SCD. As opposed to most of the existing literature, we examined associations at all levels of temperature, not just extremes such as cold spells or heat waves. Additionally, we examined the impact of temperature for the entire country, not just a selected city or metropolitan area. Our use of a fine-spatial scale (800 m) data allowed a more precise prediction of exposure, relative to previous work that used coarser (10–30 km) resolution estimates. Due to this study being embedded in the prospective NHS cohort, we were able to look at the impact of multiple potential effect modifiers, with information collected prospectively.

In conclusion, in this study of US women, increases in temperature in the week before an SCD were suggestively associated with increasing risk of SCD. Short-term decreases in temperature relative to the prior week were also associated with increased risk of SCD. These findings, paired with literature from around the world, suggest that ambient temperature may be an emerging population-level risk factor for SCD.

## Abstract

Neighborhood greenness may benefit long-term prostate cancer survivorship by promoting physical activity and social integration, and reducing stress and exposure to air pollution, noise, and extreme temperatures. We examined associations of neighborhood greenness and long-term physical and psychosocial quality of life in prostate cancer survivors in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

We included 1,437 individuals diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer between 2008 and 2016 across the United States. Neighborhood greenness within a 1230m buffer of each individual’s mailing address was measured using the Landsat satellite image-based Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI). We fit generalized linear mixed effect models to assess associations of greenness (in quintiles) with longitudinal patient reported outcome measures on prostate cancer-specific physical and psychosocial quality of life, adjusting for time-varying individual- and neighborhood-level demographic factors and clinical factors.

The greatest symptom burden was in the sexual domain. More than half of survivors reported good memory function and the lack of depressive signs at diagnosis. In fully adjusted models, cumulative average greenness since diagnosis was associated with fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms (highest quintile, Q5, vs lowest quintile, Q1: mean difference: −0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.81, −0.12). Other domains of physical quality of life, including bowel symptoms, urinary incontinence, urinary irritation, and sexual symptoms, did not differ by greenness overall. Psychosocial quality of life did not differ by greenness overall (Q5 vs Q1, odds ratio [95% CI]: memory function: 1.01 [0.61, 1.73]; lack of depressive signs: 1.10 [0.63, 1.95]; and wellbeing: 1.17 [0.71, 1.91]).

During long-term prostate cancer survivorship, cumulative average 1230m greenness since diagnosis was associated with fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms. Other domains of physical quality of life and psychosocial quality of life did not differ by greenness overall. Limitations included potential non-differential exposure measurement error and NDVI’s lack of time-activity pattern.

## Introduction

The population of prostate cancer survivors is substantial and growing. The cancer and its treatment often have long-term adverse impacts on their quality of life.1 With more than 3.6 million prostate cancer survivors living in the United States today, it is important to identify modifiable factors that may benefit the long-term survivorship experience of this vulnerable population.2,3 Neighborhood greenness, which generally refers to natural green vegetation around one’s residence, is associated with overall health, potentially through promotion of physical activity and social integration, and reduced stress and exposure to air pollution, noise, and extreme temperatures.4 It is increasingly recognized and leveraged in policy-level interventions on the environment to improve people’s physical and mental health.5–9 Given its modifiability and ubiquitous connection to many aspects of people’s lives, neighborhood greenness has the potential to influence long-term prostate cancer survivorship on a larger and more impactful scale than individual-level or interpersonal-level modifiable factors.10,11

Current evidence shows inverse associations between neighborhood greenness and prostate cancer incidence and mortality.12–14 However, the evidence on neighborhood greenness and cancer survivorship is sparse and the few existing studies found inconsistent results.15 Specifically, while a randomized trial conducted among 22 breast and lung cancer patients reported improved physical functioning after a 12-week forest therapy intervention, observational studies reported inverse associations between greenness exposure and quality of life among cancer survivors.16–18 These studies either focused on short-term greenness interventions or were cross-sectional. Consequently, they were unable to utilize longitudinal data to prospectively investigate various exposure windows that may be relevant to cancer survivors’ long-term quality of life.19 Moreover, no prior studies have been exclusively conducted among prostate cancer survivors, nor have they examined prostate cancer-specific physical quality of life or specific aspects of psychosocial quality of life.

In this study, we examined associations of neighborhood greenness and long-term physical and psychosocial quality of life among prostate cancer survivors in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study (HPFS). We also conducted analyses within subgroups defined according to age, comorbidity status, census region, population density, primary treatment, and D’Amico Risk Category at diagnosis.

## Materials and Methods

### Study Design and Population

The HPFS is a nationwide prospective cohort, consisting of 51,529 male health professionals (including dentists, pharmacists, optometrists, osteopaths, podiatrists, and veterinarians) residing across the contiguous United States (excluding Alaska and Hawaii). Through detailed biennial questionnaires since enrollment in 1986, participants self-reported their health behaviors and health outcomes, including prostate cancer diagnosis. Their mailing addresses (a mix of home and work) have been geocoded, and these locations were used to append spatially-referenced environmental exposure measures. Prostate cancer diagnoses have been validated through review of medical records and pathology reports. In addition, participants diagnosed with prostate cancer have additionally completed biennial questionnaires about their cancer’s clinical information, treatments, and quality of life.

For this analysis, participants in HPFS with a diagnosis of prostate cancer between January 2008 and December 2016 were considered for eligibility. Given differences in quality of life among metastatic prostate cancer patients, we excluded those with M1 prostate cancer (i.e., metastasis where the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body). In addition, we excluded those missing information at diagnosis on birth date, race, employment status, or neighborhood greenness, and those with a history of cancer prior to their prostate cancer diagnosis. The final analytic sample included 1,437 eligible participants (Figure 1). The study protocol was approved by the institutional review boards of Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health as well as those of participating registries as required and all study participants provided written informed consent.

### Neighborhood Greenness

Neighborhood greenness (referred to hereafter as “greenness”) is defined as the extent of photosynthetically active vegetation surrounding an address.20 It is commonly measured using a satellite image-based vegetation index called the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), which leverages both visible and near infrared light to calculate the ratio of their difference to their sum.21,22 Landsat satellite-based NDVI data were collected every two weeks at 30m x 30m resolutions.21 To account for seasonal changes and geographic difference in greenness, the seasonal averages (from January, April, July, and September) were then appended to HPFS participants’ mailing addresses. NDVI ranges from −1 to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating more vegetation, values of 0 indicating barren areas of rock, sand, or snow, and values closer to −1 indicating bodies of water. To focus on green vegetation only, negative NDVI values were assigned as zero in this analysis.13,20 We considered two buffer sizes for measuring greenness surrounding the mailing address: a 1230m buffer size representing walkable greenness (in the main analyses), and a 270m buffer size representing visible greenness from the address (in secondary analyses). In the main analyses, we modeled the time-varying cumulative average values of greenness since the time of prostate cancer diagnosis. In secondary analyses, we explored other exposure windows by modeling (1) time-fixed cumulative average NDVI values up until 3 years prior to diagnosis, (2) time-varying annual average greenness averaging NDVI values across the four seasons (with values from January, April, July, and September), and (3) time-varying annual maximum greenness (with values from July).

### Quality of Life

The outcomes of interest were prostate cancer-specific physical and psychosocial quality of life. For physical quality of life, participants responded to the Expanded Prostate Cancer Index Composite - Short Form (EPIC-26) biennially from 2010 to 2016 and Expanded Prostate Cancer Index Composite for Clinical Practice (EPIC-CP) in 2018. Both versions were developed to examine five symptom domains among localized prostate cancer patients: bowel (e.g., pain, urgency, frequency of bowel movements), urinary incontinence (e.g., urinary control, urinary dripping or leakage), urinary irritation/obstruction (e.g., pain or burning with urination, need to urinate frequently), sexual (e.g., erection quality, lack of sexual functioning), and vitality/hormonal (e.g., hot flash, lack of energy).23,24 We converted EPIC-26 into EPIC-CP scores for the analyses.25 For EPIC-CP, the summary score for each domain ranges from 1 to 12, with lower scores indicating fewer symptoms and better physical quality of life.

For psychosocial quality of life, participants self-reported their memory function, depression, and psychosocial wellbeing (referred to hereafter as “wellbeing”) via biennial follow up questionnaires. Memory function was assessed in 2008, 2012, 2016, and 2018 via the Structured Telephone Interview for Dementia Assessment-Short Form (STIDA).26,27 In this analysis, we dichotomized memory function into those who reported having no problems with memory and those who reported having at least some problems with memory. Depression and wellbeing were measured in 2008, 2012, and 2016 by the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale-Short Form (GDS-SF), a self-administered questionnaire used to assess depressive symptoms in the elderly population.28 In this analysis, we dichotomized depression (referred to as “the lack of depressive signs” in the results to aid interpretation; yes: scoring less than five points; no: those scoring five points or more) and wellbeing (no: answering no to at least one of the positive wellbeing questions in GDS-SF; yes: answering yes to all positive wellbeing questions in GDS-SF). More detailed categorizations of these measures have been described in prior work.25

### Statistical Analysis

We summarized baseline characteristics of the study population, calculated Pearson correlations between continuous measures of 1230m and 270m greenness, and descriptive statistics of the outcomes by quintiles of 1230m greenness at diagnosis. To examine the association of cumulative average greenness (categorized into quintiles) with time-varying physical domains of quality of life, we fit separate linear mixed effect models for each of the symptom domains. To examine the association of cumulative average greenness with time-varying psychosocial aspects of quality of life, we fit generalized linear mixed effect logistic regression models, which accommodated dichotomous outcomes and common features of longitudinal data, such as varying amounts of follow-up time and missingness at random.

In addition to the unadjusted models, we adjusted for three different sets of covariates, selected a priori based on previous literature, for each outcome of interest. Model 1 adjusted for the following variables at diagnosis: age (continuous) and race (White, non-White), as well as the following time-varying variables: employment status (working, not working), census region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West), season of questionnaire return (Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter), and population density (continuous, at the census track level). Model 2 additionally adjusted for the following time-varying variables: self-reported body mass index (continuous), presence of any comorbidities (including myocardial infarction, stroke, emphysema/chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, Parkinson disease, coronary artery bypass or coronary angioplasty, and diabetes; yes, no), smoking status (current, former, never), and neighborhood socioeconomic status (a summed z-score of multiple socioeconomic status metrics at the census track level).29,30 Lastly, in the fully adjusted models (Model 3), we additionally adjusted for clinical factors at diagnosis, including clinical stage (T1/T2, T3, T4/N1), Gleason score (6, 3+4, 7, 4+3, 8, 9-10), primary treatment (active surveillance, radical prostatectomy, radiation, androgen deprivation therapy, other), and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels (<4, 4-<10, 10-20, ≥20 ng/mL). Covariates were assessed through HPFS biennial questionnaires. We also conducted stratified analyses within subgroups defined according to age (<70, ≥70 years), comorbidities (no, yes), census region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West), population density (high [≥1000 people/mile2], low [<1000 people/mile2]), primary treatment (active surveillance, radical prostatectomy, radiation therapy), D’Amico Risk Category (low [stage T1c and T2a, PSA level ≤10 ng/mL, Gleason ≤6], intermediate [stage T2b, PSA level >10 and ≤20 ng/mL, Gleason 7], high [stage T2c, PSA level >20 ng/mL, Gleason ≥8]) at diagnosis.31,32

We conducted several additional analyses to assess the sensitivity of our estimates to various analytic decisions. Specifically, we (1) ended follow-up in 2016 in analyses of physical quality of life to use EPIC-26 measurements only (instead of ending follow-up in 2018 and using EPIC-CP), (2) modeled cumulative greenness exposure as a continuous variable (instead of in quintiles), (3) modeled physical quality of life scores as binary outcomes (> vs. ≤25th percentile of the domain-specific score) instead of as continuous variables, and (4) repeated the main analyses after stratifying by address type (home or work) (instead of defining exposure based on a mix of home and work addresses).

## Results

We included 1,437 eligible HPFS participants with non-metastatic prostate cancer. Table 1 summarizes baseline characteristics at diagnosis of all eligible survivors overall and stratified by 1230m greenness quintiles. At the time of diagnosis, the lowest quintile of 1230m greenness ranged from 0.00 to 0.25 and the highest quintile ranged from 0.44 to 0.66. 1230m and 270m greenness were positively correlated (r = 0.82). Overall, the mean age at diagnosis was 73.4 years (standard deviation [SD]: 6.6 years) and most participants were White (96.3%, N = 1,384). Primary treatments included radiation therapy (38.9%), radical prostatectomy (35.6%), and active surveillance (18.2%). Across increasing quintiles of greenness, population density was lower; the proportion of survivors living in the West census region was lower, while the proportion in the Northeast and South was higher; and the proportion of survivors diagnosed with Gleason 6 disease was lower.

### Physical Quality of Life

Table 2 summarizes mean scores for physical quality of life symptom domains among eligible survivors overall and stratified by 1230m greenness quintiles. Within the physical symptom domains, prostate cancer survivors reported the highest symptom burden in the sexual domain (mean: 6.46, SD: 3.14) and relatively low symptoms in other domains. Survivors in the highest quintile of greenness reported more sexual symptoms and fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms compared to the lowest quintile of greenness. We examined the mean difference in physical quality of life scores and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the association of cumulative average greenness since diagnosis and physical quality of life measured by the five symptom domains (Figure 2 and Supplementary Table 1). Within levels of the included covariates, survivors reported fewer urinary incontinence and vitality/hormonal symptoms with increasing greenness exposure. In fully adjusted models, survivors with the greatest cumulative exposure to 1230m greenness reported fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms (Q5 vs Q1: mean difference: −0.46, 95% CI: −0.81, −0.12). 1230m greenness was also associated with fewer symptoms in urinary incontinence (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −0.33, 95% CI: −0.77, 0.11), but the 95% confidence intervals included the null. Results for 270m greenness, annual average, annual maximum, and pre-diagnosis greenness were similar, but the differences in scores were smaller (Supplementary Figure 1, Supplementary Table 2).

Using cumulative averages of 1230m greenness since diagnosis, we also examined these associations from models stratified by age, comorbidities, census region, and population density at diagnosis (Table 3). Among survivors in the Northeast region, greenness was associated with fewer symptoms in urinary incontinence (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −0.98, 95% CI: −1.80, −0.16). Greenness was also associated with fewer sexual symptoms for survivors in the South region (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −1.27, 95% CI: −2.42, −0.11). Lastly, greenness was associated with fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms among those diagnosed at 70 years or older (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −0.63, 95% CI: −1.16, −0.11), with comorbidity at diagnosis (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −1.04, 95% CI: −1.97, −0.10), in the Midwest region (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −1.18, 95% CI: −2.13, −0.23), or in areas with low population density (Q5 vs. Q1: mean difference: −0.48, 95% CI: −0.91, −0.05). Supplementary Table 3 summarizes associations from models stratified by primary treatment and D’Amico risk classification, but estimates were imprecise.

In the sensitivity analyses, results remained qualitatively similar when we (1) ended follow-up in 2016 to use EPIC-26 measurements of physical quality of life only (Supplementary Table 4), (2) modeled cumulative greenness as a continuous measure instead of as quintiles (Supplementary Table 5), (3) modeled physical quality of life as binary outcomes instead of as continuous outcomes (Supplementary Table 6), and (4) examined associations from models stratified by address type (Supplementary Table 7).

### Psychosocial Quality of Life

Table 2 summarizes proportions reporting good psychosocial quality of life among eligible survivors overall and stratified by 1230m greenness quintiles. Most prostate cancer survivors reported good memory function and lack of depressive signs, while less than half reported wellbeing at diagnosis. At diagnosis, more survivors in the highest quintile of greenness reported the lack of depressive signs and having poor memory function compared to the lowest quintile of greenness. Across increasing quintiles of greenness, proportions of survivors reporting wellbeing decreased at diagnosis. We estimated the odds ratios (OR) and 95% CIs for the association of cumulative average greenness since diagnosis and each of memory function, the lack of depressive signs, and wellbeing (Figure 2 and Supplementary Table 1). These aspects of psychosocial quality of life did not differ by 1230m greenness overall (memory function: Q5 vs Q1 odds ratio [95% CI]: 1.01 [0.61, 1.73]; lack of depressive signs: Q5 vs Q1 odds ratio [95% CI]: 1.10 [0.63, 1.95]; and wellbeing (Q5 vs Q1 odds ratio [95% CI]: 1.17 [0.71, 1.91]).and showed no clear trends with increasing greenness exposure. In fully adjusted models, estimates for 270m greenness suggested an association with lower wellbeing (Q5 vs. Q1: OR: 0.70, 95% CI: 0.42, 1.15), though confidence intervals were wide. When examining annual maximum greenness for both 1230m and 270m buffer sizes, higher greenness exposure was associated with lower memory function (Supplementary Figure 1, Supplementary Table 2), though precision was limited for 270m greenness.

Using cumulative averages of 1230m greenness since diagnosis, we also examined these associations from models stratified by age, comorbidities, census region, and population density at diagnosis (Table 3). Among those in the West region, greenness was associated with better memory function (Q5 vs. Q1: OR: 4.69, 95% CI: 1.28, 17.18). Supplementary Table 6 summarizes associations from stratified models by primary treatment and D’Amico risk classification, but due to limited sample size for some of the subgroups, confidence intervals were wide. In the sensitivity analyses, results remained qualitatively similar when we examined associations from stratified models by address type (Supplementary Table 7).

## Discussion

In this cohort of non-metastatic prostate cancer survivors, cumulative 1230m greenness exposure since diagnosis was associated with fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms. Additionally, inverse associations between 1230m greenness and physical symptoms in the urinary incontinence, sexual, and vitality/hormonal domains were observed among certain subsets of the population, defined at diagnosis by age, comorbidity status, census region, and population density. Overall, psychosocial quality of life did not meaningfully differ by greenness.

Literature on greenness and prostate cancer-specific physical quality of life is limited, but prior studies have examined greenness and physical quality of life more generally among cancer survivors. Consistent with our findings, one randomized trial reported that being assigned to forest therapy (conducted once a week for 12 weeks) improved physical functioning and vitality among 22 breast and lung cancer patients who otherwise were city dwellers with limited access to green environments.16 Evidence shows that greenness may encourage physical activity.4,15 This mechanism could explain our findings of an inverse association between greenness and vitality/hormonal symptoms. Two cross-sectional studies that examined greenness and general physical quality of life have reported inconclusive results.17,18 Notably, these studies examined physical quality of life as a summary outcome. By contrast, our study examined prostate cancer-specific symptom domains, which captured more granular relationships and identified specific aspects of physical quality of life that were associated with greenness. Prior studies reported inverse associations between greenness and prostate cancer mortality overall, and especially in high population density areas.14,33 In our examination of prostate cancer-specific quality of life, we found that 1230m greenness was associated with fewer vitality/hormonal symptoms in low population density areas. Additionally, we observed an inverse association between 1230m greenness and vitality/hormonal symptoms specifically among those 70 years or older and those with comorbidities. Considering that prostate cancer survivors with comorbidities and older age at diagnosis are already susceptible to lower physical functioning, our stratified findings highlight that these particularly vulnerable subgroups experience better physical quality of life with more exposure to greenness.34,35

Prior evidence for psychosocial health benefits of greenness mostly stems from trials conducted in non-cancer populations, in which interventions involving greenness improved mental health outcomes.7–9 Few prior studies have evaluated greenness and psychosocial quality of life among cancer survivors, and no studies, to our knowledge, have examined greenness and the specific psychosocial aspects of quality of life considered here among prostate cancer survivors.15 While results for 1230m greenness and psychosocial quality of life were generally null, our secondary analyses showed a weak association between 270m greenness and poorer wellbeing, though estimates were imprecise. This is consistent with a prior cross-sectional study that reported an association between greenness and lower mental quality of life in 2,477 cancer patients.17 However, future studies should further examine this relationship. For memory function, we observed that 1230m greenness was associated with better memory function specifically among those who reside in the West region. Considering those residing in the West region generally had the lowest greenness exposure compared to the rest of the United States, greenness exposure within this subgroup may additionally capture socioeconomic disparities and inequitable access to greenness. While our estimates were fairly unstable, this is similar to the results of two randomized trials that examined short-term nature-related interventions and cancer survivors’ post-treatment cognitive abilities.16,36 Greenness is proposed to benefit health through psychological processes, as it may foster social connections, reduce stress and anxiety.4 Our results might additionally point to the relationship between greenness and long-term memory function among prostate cancer survivors, but future research is needed to confirm these findings.

There are some limitations to consider. First, using NDVI as our measure for greenness, we did not have information on time-activity patterns of the participants regarding time spent engaging with nature or information to differentiate whether greenness represented parks, trees, farms, or vacant lots. Second, NDVI values were geocoded based on survivors’ questionnaire mailing addresses, which included a mix of home and work addresses within this cohort. However, this is unlikely to introduce bias, as questionnaire address type is unlikely to be associated with post-diagnosis quality of life.13 We conducted sensitivity analyses stratified by address type and results did not meaningfully differ between those with home and work addresses. Third, while we adjusted for demographic, epidemiologic, and clinical factors, we could not rule out the possibility of having other known risk factors, such as individual-level SES or lifestyle behaviors, partially explaining the observed associations. However, we adjusted for neighborhood socioeconomic status and the minimally and fully adjusted estimates were generally similar (Supplementary Table 1). Fourth, our results may not be generalizable to other populations with different distributions of demographics and greenness exposures. Lastly, we were limited in our ability to precisely estimate these associations in certain subgroups.

## Conclusions

In summary, among individuals with non-metastatic prostate cancer, cumulative 1230m greenness exposure since diagnosis was associated with fewer long-term vitality/hormonal symptoms overall, while psychosocial quality of life did not meaningfully differ by greenness. This is one of the first prospective cohort studies to examine the associations between greenness and long-term physical and psychosocial quality of life among prostate cancer survivors specifically. Focusing on long-term cancer survivorship is especially relevant for prostate cancer survivors, given their high survival.37 Moreover, using longitudinal measurements, we examined multiple exposure windows of greenness, including cumulative average since diagnosis, immediate (annual average and annual maximum), and 3-years pre-diagnosis greenness. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm our findings, especially for subgroup analyses defined by relevant clinical factors for prostate cancer survivors. Additionally, future studies could examine subgroups defined by socioeconomic status and consider the extent to which the relationship between greenness and quality of life may be mediated by certain factors. The use of global positioning system or Google street view for exposure measurement could further elucidate the mechanisms through which greenness may relate to survivors’ quality of life and the exposure areas most relevant for this population. The potential impact of nature on cancer survivorship is increasingly acknowledged, but current literature and utilization of this environmental modifiable factor is still underexplored.15,38 This study generated hypothesis for future interventions to leverage greenness as an environmental, contextual modifiable factor that could promote long-term physical and psychosocial quality of life of prostate cancer survivors on a broad scale.
